query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Mo with Ta in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will reduce the detrimental electronegativity difference and improve room-temperature plasticity while maintaining the high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy composed equiatomically of Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf, and Mo with a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa and limited plasticity attributed to high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Replace approximately 20–40% of the Mo content with Ta.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compressive testing environment, where compressive yield strength and ductility (plastic strain to failure) are evaluated.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of the alloy’s chemical composition leads to a reduced average electronegativity difference. This substitution is expected to alter the dislocation core structure, potentially producing a more compact core similar to that observed in alloys with balanced BCC and HCP element ratios.
generation.mechanism: Replacing a fraction of Mo with Ta diminishes the overall electronegativity mismatch. This reduction is theorized to lower lattice distortion and decrease the dislocation core energy, thereby permitting more uniform dislocation motion and an improved ductility without significantly reducing the high yield strength characteristic of the BCC structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to retain a compressive yield strength close to 1700 MPa while exhibiting enhanced plasticity (increased strain to failure) relative to the unmodified equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with high Mo content that suffers from limited plasticity due to an increased electronegativity difference.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only within an optimal substitution range (approximately 20–40% Mo replacement by Ta); deviations outside this range may either insufficiently reduce the electronegativity difference or compromise strength if too much Mo is replaced.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal substitution level and the resulting changes in dislocation core structure have not been determined and require focused experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of alloys with varying levels of Mo substitution by Ta (0%, 20%, 30%, and 40%). Perform room-temperature compressive tests to measure yield strength and ductility, and conduct microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM) to assess dislocation core structures.
measurements: Dislocation core structure via transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Electronegativity mapping and lattice distortion measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any alloy with substituted Ta shows either a decrease in yield strength exceeding 10% below the 1719 MPa baseline or fails to display a statistically significant increase in plasticity compared to the unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis is refuted.

## Abstract
AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties Poor ductility is a major drawback of otherwise promising
